newsitem.title: MACEDONIA: Macedonian opposition to push for early elections.
newsitem.headline: Macedonian opposition to push for early elections.

text.p: The leaders of Macedonia's main opposition coalition said on Tuesday they would use their strong showing in local elections to try to force an early parliamentary poll.
By Tuesday morning, the Social Democratic Alliance (SDAM) had claimed victory in 13 councils -- just two more than the main opposition coalition led by the right-wing VMRO-DPME.
But VRMO said it had won some of the biggest towns and was leading in three of the four districts in the capital Skopje.

"The election is a coup against the government," opposition spokesman Dragi Ivanovski told Reuters. "We have proven our electoral support and now we can go ahead with our campaign for early elections."
Even Prime Minister Branko Crvenkovski's own party conceded the results placed the opposition in a strong position to renew its stalled campaign to oust the government.

"On the local level, the opposition now has the opportunity to fight for early parliamentary elections," the ruling Social Democratic Alliance's General-Secretary Ljupco Popovski admitted on state radio.

The party also insisted it had won the election by seizing the most number of municipalities in the first round of voting, but privately party officials say they are disappointed and have predicted a shakeup of the senior leadership as a result.
Early results indicated most of the 124 councils would have to go through run-off elections on December 1 to decide the outcome.
The unofficial results did not take account of opposition appeals expected over allegations of fraud and widespread reports of irregularities on the electoral lists.

European observers confirmed that large numbers of people were unable to find their names on electoral lists, and said the problem had prevented as many as 25 percent of the would-be voters from participating in the poll.
The town-based municipalities hold the lion's share of the nation's 1.4 million voters and analysts said opposition victories there would hand them substantial electoral clout.

"This might be local elections, but like so many by-elections in Western democracies, everyone is treating this as a mid-term referendum on the government's performance," said one Western analyst who declined to be named. "So far the results have been pretty disappointing for them."

VMRO and its allies boycotted the 1994 parliamentary elections and has no parliamentary representation. Earlier this year the government foiled a VMRO bid to force early elections, not due until 1998, with a petition of over 200,000 signatures.
Ivanovski said the local election results had given them the backing they needed to resurrect the petition which is bogged down in the constitutional court.

A key campaign issue was the economy. The government took credit for nursing Macedonia to independence from its place in the former Yugoslav federation and introducing widespread privatisation and a Western-leaning economy.

Ivanovski described the privatisation scheme as "communists flogging the family jewels," and said it had led to corruption and poverty. VMRO argued for a more measured pace of economic reform, based on the East German model.
